title: Humor in AI: Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Benchmarks for Cartoon Captioning (Zhang et al., NeurIPS 2024)
mechanism: New Yorker caption contest, 250M votes. Claude-3-Opus beat the contest top-10 captions 54.4% overall (GPT-4o 44.5%) but crowd preference 35.4% vs expert (ex-New Yorker cartoon editor) 1.6%.
example: Expert found human captions 'better phrased and more concise'; LLM captions 'too verbose', less diverse, sometimes ignore visual details, and lean on invented-word modification which readers rate low.
rule: Cut the line to the fewest words; the joke must be about what is in the scene; winners support several readings at once. Crowd taste flatters the model, an expert editor does not: judge with the sharpest reader available.
llm_failure: Verbose, low diversity, off-context, word-play by modification. SFT hurt, RLHF (PPO) drove win rate against the median from 24.7% to 5.0%; best-of-N cut diversity. Image input gave mixed results.

title: A Robot Walks into a Bar: LLMs as creativity support tools for comedy (Mirowski et al., FAccT 2024)
mechanism: 20 comedians, workshops. Verdict: 'cruise ship comedy material from the 1950s, but a bit less racist'. Output generic, no perspective so no risk, linear, lacks urgency; safety tuning removes edge and dark material.
example: 'It had no perspective, so it couldn't take any risks in terms of jokes'; 'the only thing again that is funny in what I gave you is the joke I put into the prompting'; 'If you make something that fits everybody, it probably will end up being nobody's favorite thing'; 'comedy is all about subtext'; 'usually it can serve in a setup capacity. I more often than not provide the punchline'.
rule: Use the model for structure, a vomit draft and the setup; the writer supplies the punchline, the point of view and the specific detail. A joke needs someone who risks something saying it.
llm_failure: Generic words, no risk, tropes regurgitated, straight-laced linear structure, wrong specifics (set in Sweden, names not Swedish), refuses or softens dark and offensive angles.

title: What happened when 20 comedians got AI to write their routines (MIT Tech Review)
mechanism: Press account of the DeepMind study. The one LLM joke the reporter called better was a wordplay tied to the show's own topic; comedians did not single out joke hits. Chakrabarty (Columbia): humour rests on surprise and incongruity, at odds with next-word prediction.
example: 'a vomit draft that I know that I'm going to have to iterate on and improve'
rule: What the comedians kept was structure and a draft to rewrite, not finished jokes; a joke tied to the specific occasion beat a free-floating one.
llm_failure: Bland, generic, boring; safety filters bar dark/offensive humour; the effort was not worth it for some. No account of which individual LLM jokes landed and why: that evidence is thin.

title: How funny is ChatGPT? A comparison of human- and A.I.-produced jokes (Gorenz & Schwarz, PLOS ONE 2024)
mechanism: GPT-3.5, 20 outputs per prompt, blind raters. Roast-joke task preferred 73% of the time (beat ~87% of laypeople); acronyms 58%; fill-in-blank 50.5%. Onion-style headlines rated as funny as real Onion ones.
example: Top headline (ChatGPT): 'Local Man Discovers New Emotion, Still Can't Describe It Properly'. Also: 'Man Achieves Personal Best in Avoiding Eye Contact With Neighbors During Awkward Elevator Ride'.
rule: Hits came from a tight form (a fixed headline template, a short roast against a stated awkward scenario) with a concrete situation and a small human frailty as target; the set-up was supplied and many candidates were generated and sampled. Generate many, pick few.
llm_failure: Caveats: human comparison was lay people for Study 1, only 3 prompts per task, prompts and examples did heavy lifting, three random responses (not the best) shown, no joke-feature analysis. Does not show models write good jokes unprompted. The earlier Jentzsch finding (25 repeated jokes) came from the open-ended 'tell me a joke' prompt.

title: USC press piece on Gorenz & Schwarz
mechanism: Same study, press version: 105 humans (945+ jokes) vs ChatGPT 180 jokes; ~70% of ratings favoured ChatGPT.
example: Prompts were acronyms, fill-in-the-blank ('A lesser known room in the White House'), and a roast reply to an awkward scenario.
rule: The winning tasks were constrained and situational, not 'be funny'.
llm_failure: Study 2 (professional-grade comparison) is a tie, not a win.

title: Assessing LLMs in Humor: Oogiri generation and evaluation (AAAI-26)
mechanism: LLM responses rated between low- and mid-tier human. Six rating dimensions; models score on Novelty, humans reward Empathy.
example: 'LLMs prioritize Novelty, whereas humans prioritize Empathy.'
rule: A strange idea is not enough: the reader must recognise something true in it. Surprise plus shared feeling.
llm_failure: Chases the unexpected for its own sake and does not check that it resonates; single funny/not-funny judgments hide this.

title: Oogiri-Master: linguistic features vs funniness (via aggregator summary)
mechanism: Correlational feature study of high- vs low-rated responses: perspective shift d=0.50, ambiguity exploitation d=0.42, incongruity resolution d=0.36, shorter responses d=-0.28, fewer words not in the prompt; surprisal and semantic distance only minimal effect. Benign violation and metaphor named predictive, no sizes.
rule: Funnier lines are shorter, re-use the prompt's own words, shift the viewpoint and resolve their incongruity; raw randomness or distance from the prompt does not predict funny.
llm_failure: Models tend toward length and lexical novelty, the wrong direction. Understanding benchmark only, Japanese only, correlational; aggregator page, not the paper itself.

title: Pun Unintended: LLMs and the Illusion of Humor Understanding (Zangari et al., EMNLP 2025)
mechanism: Detection above 0.83 on the old benchmark drops 15% on common pun templates and 50% on PunBreak (broken puns). GPT-4o accuracy 0.33 on homophone-swapped non-puns: it calls anything pun-shaped a pun by surface pattern.
example: Fine-tuned RoBERTa 92.5 F1 on the original set, 64.0 on a new one; 171 of 173 template items were puns.
rule: A pun works only if both senses fit the context and the sounds really match; check the two readings by hand, not by 'sounds like a pun'.
llm_failure: Pattern-matches pun templates; mis-identifies the pun word pair; misses context. Generation not tested here (cited as weaker than human). Mechanisms (tokenisation, sycophancy) are hypotheses.

title: Hessel et al.: Do Androids Laugh at Electric Sheep? (Cornell news)
mechanism: New Yorker caption tasks: best model matched caption to cartoon at 62% vs 94% for humans; human explanations of why it is funny preferred about 2:1 over AI explanations. Links between image and caption are 'indirect, playful, and reference lots of real-world entities and norms'.
rule: The joke lives in the gap between the thing shown and a real-world norm; name the norm, not the gag.
llm_failure: Misses indirect references and cannot explain why a joke works, so it cannot tell its own hit from its own miss. Press page; paper full text not read.

title: ChatGPT is fun, but it is not funny! (Jentzsch & Kersting)
mechanism: Over 90% of 1,008 outputs were the same 25 jokes (GPT-3.5).
rule: Never ask for 'a joke'; give the situation, the target and the form. Already in dialogue-and-humour.md.

title: HumorGen preprint tags (via search summary)
mechanism: Preferred jokes tagged incongruity 85.2%, absurdity 84.9%, surprise 57.2%, wordplay 42.0%; low agreement (alpha ~0.41).
rule: Suggestive only: incongruity and absurdity track wins; wordplay is the minority.
llm_failure: Weak evidence; do not quote the numbers without reading the paper (the search result named arXiv 2604.09629, not fetched).

title: Benign violation theory (McGraw & Warren 2010; McGraw et al. 2012), via search summary
mechanism: Humour comes from a violation seen as benign at the same time. Benign via: an alternative norm, weak commitment to the violated norm, or psychological distance. Severe violations (tragedy) are funnier when distant in time, place, person or hypothetical; mild mishaps are funnier when close. A 2023 replication supported the benign half but not the distance effect.
rule: Dark jokes need a safety valve: distance, a character who is not hurt, or a frame in which the harm is small. Mishaps want closeness; atrocities want distance.
llm_failure: Safety-tuned models cut the violation entirely, leaving the benign half only (cruise-ship material); or add a violation with no benign frame.

title: Gallows Humor (Engines of Narrative)
mechanism: A small comic or incongruous image placed after a dark passage reframes the danger as smaller and gives readers enough relief to go on.
example: Moby-Dick ch. 38: Starbuck sees the whale as a goldfish; Lorrie Moore, 'Terrific Mother': after a baby's accidental death the boyfriend proposes 'I'm going to marry you till you puke'; the gravediggers in Hamlet; the porter in Macbeth.
rule: Keep it small (a micro-instance), put it after the dark beat, let a character who is suffering make it, and let it help them carry on rather than dismiss the loss. It can run through a whole grief arc.
llm_failure: Not stated in the source. Observed elsewhere: models either refuse the dark beat or stack a joke on top as if to cancel it.

title: Hitchhiker's Guide tone (Shmoop), via search summary
mechanism: Deadpan: the performer never signals 'this is a joke'; Cleese's memorial sketch makes a sad moment funny by saying terrible things without smiling.
example: Monty Python memorial sketch (Cleese on Chapman).
rule: Dry and gallows humour share one rule: do not flag the joke. The narrator's face stays still.
llm_failure: Study-guide level source. Models explain or underline the joke, or add an exclamation; see the Mirowski 'subtext' quote.

title: Laughing Stock: Ron Gilbert (Kill Screen)
humour_kind: character humour / escalation in games; running gags
mechanism: Gilbert: comedy is about timing, which a game gives up to the player; adventure dialogue keeps the back-and-forth. Jokes should be funny, reveal character and help the player with the puzzle. Humour grows from building a character, not from non-sequiturs.
example: Guybrush, the hero who sees himself as more heroic than the world does (per related interview summaries, not read).
rule: A game joke must do a second job (character or puzzle information) and be tied to what is on screen; the target is the hero's self-image, not the hero. The article gives no rule for frequency.
llm_failure: Not addressed. Random non-sequitur wackiness is the failure he avoids.

source: none (writer's own knowledge, not fetched; verify before quoting)
title: Taxonomy notes: classic examples
humour_kind: dry, understatement, bathos, callback, running gag, escalation, anti-joke
mechanism: Dry/understatement: the narration is calmer than the event. Bathos: build a high register, drop to a mundane detail. Callback: pay off an earlier detail in a changed context. Escalation: each beat the same logic, bigger. Anti-joke: set a joke shape, deliver a flat truth.
example: Adams: the ships 'hung in the sky in much the same way that bricks don't'; Wodehouse: 'If not actually disgruntled, he was far from being gruntled'; Pratchett footnotes (already covered).
rule: One logic per joke; the funny word last; a callback needs a changed context or it is a repeat; escalation must obey its own rule.
llm_failure: Unverified here. Common observation: explains the joke; puts three items in the list regardless; ends on the moral instead of the reveal.
